question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The system is presented as an assistive musical application for visually impaired people, motivated by interviews about difficulties learning music and using existing software. The design focuses on a utilitarian goal (accessible music composition without memorizing scores, avoiding embarrassing sounds) and then incorporates enjoyable, tangible interaction using familiar objects. This aligns best with a mostly utility-first design where the primary assistive mechanic is designed first and fun is incorporated, rather than a game or entertainment-first approach.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) unstructured play (i.e., no rules, making art),
        (2) semi-structured play (i.e., playground activities),
        (3) flexible structure with rules (i.e., improv),
        (4) flexible game (i.e., board game with house rules),
        (5) game with rigid rules (i.e., video game)
reasoning: Participants freely arranged tangible objects on a table to compose music, with no mention of explicit rules, scoring, or win conditions; the activity is exploratory and creative rather than a structured or rule-bound game, aligning best with unstructured play.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely skill-based (i.e., trivia, sports),
        (2) mostly skill-based (i.e., mario kart),
        (3) equally skill and chance-based (i.e., catan),
        (4) mostly chance-based (i.e., Uno),
        (5) entirely chance-based (i.e., all dice)
reasoning: Participants are composing music by deliberately placing tangible objects to create melodies and phrases; there is no randomization or probabilistic mechanic described. Outcomes (the resulting music) are fully determined by users' intentional actions, making the task entirely skill/choice-based rather than chance-based.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely solo (i.e., solitaire),
        (2) mostly solo (i.e., playing against AI in single-player StarCraft),
        (3) mix of solo and social affordances (i.e., animal crossing),
        (4) mostly social, but aspects are independent (i.e., house on hill haunt transition),
        (5) entirely social (i.e., tag)
reasoning: The application explicitly supports both single-user use and two-user collaborative composing on the same tabletop interface, indicating a mix of solo and social affordances rather than being purely solo or purely social.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely turn-based (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) follows a set of steps (i.e., viticulture's dynamic turn ordering),
        (3) turns are taken, but some actions can be taken at any time (i.e., pandemic),
        (4) most actions can be taken at any time, but there are some phases (i.e., PvP death reset timer),
        (5) entirely simultaneous (i.e., race)
reasoning: The system is a continuous music composition interface where users freely place and adjust tangible objects on a table while percussion is continuously replayed, and gestures can change tempo at any moment. In the two-user condition, both participants act concurrently on the shared space. There is no indication of discrete turns, ordered steps, or enforced phases; actions appear to be possible at any time and effectively simultaneous, fitting category 5 best among the options.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely synchronous (i.e., real time strategy game),
        (2) mostly synchronous with a few asynchronous affordances (i.e., league of legends),
        (3) equal mix of synchronous and asynchronous affordances (i.e., helldivers 2),
        (4) mostly asynchronous with few synchronous affordances (i.e. cookie clicker),
        (5) entirely asynchronous (i.e., chess by postage mail)
reasoning: The system uses Kinect to continuously detect object positions and gestures, with users composing while percussion is continuously replayed and tempo adjusted in real time via hand-waving. Collaboration occurs live at the same tabletop. These features indicate an entirely synchronous, real-time interactive system rather than asynchronous play or turn-taking.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely competitive (i.e., spit card game),
        (2) mostly competitive, but sometimes collaboration is important (i.e., forbidden island),
        (3) mix of competitive and collaborative (i.e., mario party 2 vs 2 mini-games),
        (4) mostly collaborative (i.e., animal crossing),
        (5) entirely collaborative (i.e., pandemic)
reasoning: The system is a music composition application where users work together to compose music; the two-user evaluation explicitly studies collaboration and communication, with no mention of competition or opposing goals, indicating an entirely collaborative design.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely symmetrical (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) mostly symmetrical (i.e., undertale's differing NPC behaviors based on previous playthroughs),
        (3) both symmetrical and asymmetrical (i.e., pandemic with its similar turn structure but different character abilities),
        (4) mostly asymmetrical (i.e., tag),
        (5) entirely asymmetrical (i.e., keep talking, nobody explodes)
reasoning: All users have access to the same interaction mechanics (placing clips/strings, using AR markers, waving to change tempo). In two-user mode, both participants can perform the same actions with the same tools; there are no differentiated roles, abilities, or rule sets. This indicates an entirely symmetrical design.
